questions.title: Tell me about yourself.
questions.answer: Sources: start with the present and say why you're well qualified (64 Toughest Q1). Two or three minutes covering years/function, education, main accomplishments and work style (1point3acres). Format: name, major, technical strength, a standout project with a metric, why this role (1point3acres 'Crack the BQ').
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** A 60–120 second pitch, present → past → future, that matches your background to *this* DV role. It is not your life story; it is the trailer for the rest of the interview.

| Part | What to say (DV version) |
| --- | --- |
| **Present** | M.S. student in EECS at NTHU, focused on [digital design / verification]. |
| **Past (evidence)** | 2–3 projects that map to the JD: UVM testbench for an AXI4 2-master/3-slave crossbar, a 3-clock-domain NTT accelerator signed off with JasperGold CDC, a 16-bit RISC CPU with caches. Give one number each, e.g. [N tests / X% functional coverage / Y bugs]. |
| **Future (fit)** | Why this role: you want to own verification of [GPU / interconnect] blocks, and this internship is the next step. |
| **Hook** | End with a question or an offer: "Happy to go deeper into any of these." |

### Sample answer
> I'm a master's student in EECS at National Tsing Hua University, and most of my work is in design verification. My main project is a UVM testbench for an AXI4 crossbar with 2 masters and 3 slaves. I built the agents, a reference-model scoreboard and a coverage model, and closed [X%] functional coverage across [N] tests. I also verified a 3-clock-domain NTT accelerator and signed off its CDC with JasperGold, and I designed a 16-bit RISC CPU with caches, so I know the design side as well. I'm applying for this DV internship because I want to verify [GPU / interconnect] IP at real scale, and I'm happy to go deeper into any of these projects.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Can you communicate concisely and in a structured way?
- Have you read the JD, and do you pick the experiences that match it? (1point3acres: 'did you read the job requirements, are you that person?')
- Your technical focus, which they will use to steer later questions.

### Pitfalls
- Rambling chronologically from your undergrad onwards (the 64 Toughest calls this the #1 trap).
- Reading your resume aloud, or listing tools without saying what you did with them.
- Personal details that have nothing to do with the job.
- Running past 2 minutes. Stop and let them choose a thread.

### Follow-ups
- **Which project are you most proud of?** Have your best STAR story ready (see the 'most challenging project' question).
- **What was your role on that team?** Use 'I' for your own contributions and 'we' only for team results.
- **Why verification rather than design?** Have a one-sentence answer ready that ties to something you enjoyed in a project.

questions.title: What are your greatest strengths?
questions.answer: Have a memorised list of strengths, each with a recent achievement, and pick the ones matching the interviewer's needs. The traits employers look for include track record, intelligence, integrity, fit, likeability, communication, dedication, clear goals, enthusiasm and confidence (64 Toughest Q2 / 1point3acres #6). 1point3acres: say which trait fits the role best and close with 'good fit'.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Pick 2–3 strengths that match the role's needs and back each one with a specific, recent example. Be confident without bragging.

| Element | DV example |
| --- | --- |
| **Strength** | Systematic debugging: I narrow a failure from scoreboard mismatch → transaction → cycle. |
| **Evidence (S/T)** | In the AXI crossbar TB a random test failed only with [seed N] after [X] transactions. |
| **Evidence (A)** | I added transaction IDs to the monitor logs, diffed them against the reference model, and found an arbitration corner case at [condition]. |
| **Payoff (R)** | Fixed in [time]. I added a directed test and a coverage cross so it can't regress. Same skill is what a DV intern does daily. |

### Sample answer
> I'd say my biggest strength is systematic debugging. In my AXI4 crossbar testbench, one random seed failed after about [N] transactions. I didn't add prints everywhere. I added transaction IDs to the monitor and compared the observed stream against the reference model, which led me to a [write-response ordering] corner case when [two masters targeted the same slave]. I also added a coverage cross for that scenario so it can't regress silently. A second strength is that I learn tools fast: I went from never having used JasperGold to a clean CDC sign-off on a 3-clock-domain design in [X weeks].

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Self-awareness: do you know what you're good at?
- Fit: do your strengths match the job's 'greatest wants and needs' (64 Toughest)?
- Credibility: is there evidence behind each claim?

### Pitfalls
- Listing adjectives (hard-working, passionate) with no story behind them.
- False modesty, or sounding arrogant.
- Naming strengths that don't matter for DV.

### Follow-ups
- **Give me another example of that strength.** Have a second story ready from a different project.
- **What would your teammates say your strength is?** Give a consistent answer, ideally a quote from real feedback.
- **How does that strength help on this team?** Connect it to their flow: regressions, debug, coverage closure.

questions.title: What is your greatest weakness? (Where could you use some improvement?)
questions.answer: Pick a real weakness you're actively fixing and show what you're doing (1point3acres #5). 1point3acres BQ thread: a harmless weakness, the project where you discovered it, the lesson, and how you applied it later. The 64 Toughest Q3/Q44 alternatives are to talk about likes/dislikes, or an area you want to grow in that isn't essential to the job.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Name a real but non-critical weakness, show the moment you noticed it, and spend most of the answer on the concrete steps you're taking and the measurable improvement.

| STAR | Sample (DV scenario, adapt the [placeholders]) |
| --- | --- |
| **S**ituation | Early in the CPU project I [over-committed / under-communicated / jumped into coding before planning]. Example: I wrote the testbench before writing a test plan. |
| **T**ask | Coverage holes surfaced late; I had to rework [N] tests. I needed a habit, not a one-off fix. |
| **A**ction | Now I write a verification plan first (features → checks → coverage points), review it with a peer, and track progress weekly. |
| **R**esult | On the AXI crossbar project coverage closure took [X% less time] and the plan doubled as my report. I still catch myself wanting to code first, but the habit sticks. |

### Sample answer
> Earlier in my master's, my weakness was jumping straight into coding before planning. On my RISC CPU project I started writing testbench code before I had a verification plan, and I found coverage holes late, which cost me [about two weeks] of rework. Since then I always write a short verification plan first, listing each feature, how it's checked and which coverage points prove it, and I have a labmate review it. On my AXI crossbar testbench that made closure much smoother, and the plan became the backbone of my final report. I still feel the pull to code first, but now the plan comes first by habit.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Self-awareness and honesty.
- Coachability: what do you do with feedback?
- Whether the weakness is a dealbreaker for this role.

### Pitfalls
- Humble-brags like 'I'm a perfectionist' or 'I work too hard'. 1point3acres calls this deceiving, and interviewers have heard it countless times.
- Naming a core skill of the job (e.g. 'I'm bad at debugging').
- Describing the weakness without saying what you're doing about it.
- Note: the 64 Toughest PDF suggests saying you have none. Most modern interviewers, including big-tech DV teams, score that as evasive. Give a real, managed weakness instead.

### Follow-ups
- **What's another weakness?** Have a second, smaller one, e.g. public speaking, and how you're practising.
- **How would your advisor describe it?** Stay consistent with what you said, and be honest.
- **How do you know you've improved?** Give a metric or an outcome, e.g. fewer late surprises or less rework.

questions.title: Why do you want to work at our company? (What do you know about us?)
questions.answer: Tests whether you've done homework; research annual reports, trade press, contacts (64 Toughest Q11). Sugarac: product you use + culture + growth. 1point3acres: mission matches career goal; requirements match background; never mention money or empty grand claims; personal angle works best.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Show that you did your homework. Connect a specific fact about the company and its product or team to your own experience and goals, and avoid generic praise and money.

| Ingredient | Example |
| --- | --- |
| **Company fact** | e.g. NVIDIA: GPUs/SoCs for AI and graphics, very large designs, heavy use of UVM, formal and emulation. Use what you actually learned from the JD, talks or engineers. |
| **Team/role fact** | The JD mentions [interconnect / memory subsystem / formal / CDC]. |
| **Your link** | Your AXI crossbar UVM TB and JasperGold CDC sign-off map directly to that. |
| **What you want to learn** | Verification at a scale a university project can't reach: [emulation, coverage at SoC level]. |

### Sample answer
> I've used NVIDIA GPUs in [my coursework / ML experiments], but the main reason is the engineering. Your chips are some of the largest and most complex designs anywhere, so verification is a first-class discipline there. The JD mentions [interconnect and memory-subsystem verification], which is exactly what my AXI4 crossbar UVM testbench was about, and I also did CDC sign-off with JasperGold on a multi-clock accelerator. I want to learn how verification scales to [SoC-level coverage, emulation, formal at scale], and I think I can contribute from day one on block-level testbench work.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Research: do you know what they actually do?
- Genuine motivation versus 'any job will do'.
- Fit between your skills and their needs (1point3acres: mission ↔ career goal, requirements ↔ background).

### Pitfalls
- Talking about money, perks or prestige ('it's the biggest company').
- Facts copied from the homepage without a personal link.
- Big claims like 'change the world'. The 1point3acres thread warns interviewers aren't fooled by them.

### Follow-ups
- **What do you know about our products?** Name one or two and say something specific, e.g. how they relate to the IP you'd verify.
- **Which other companies are you interviewing with?** Be honest in general terms and say why this one is your first choice.
- **What would you change about our product?** Be careful. Ask a question back rather than criticise.

questions.title: Why design verification? Why this role rather than design (or your original major)?
questions.answer: 1point3acres: 'Why are you major X but want SDE/DS?' Tell what related project or internship you did, its impact, and that you enjoyed the output. #83: 'Why do you want to work in the ___ industry?' Crack the BQ: explain from your own experience of doing the work, and say why your current path isn't enough (without complaining).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Use a concrete moment where you enjoyed verification work, the impact it had, and evidence you're good at it. Present DV as a positive choice, not a fallback from design.

| STAR | Sample (DV scenario, adapt the [placeholders]) |
| --- | --- |
| **S**ituation | During [the RISC CPU project] I did both RTL and verification. |
| **T**ask | Decide where to specialise for my career. |
| **A**ction | I noticed I enjoyed the verification half more: designing stimulus to break the design, writing a reference model, chasing a failing seed. I went deeper with UVM (AXI crossbar) and formal/CDC (JasperGold). |
| **R**esult | Bugs found in verification are the ones that would otherwise cost a respin, and that impact motivates me. My design background makes me a better verifier because I can read the RTL and predict where it breaks. |

### Sample answer
> I've done both. I designed a 16-bit RISC CPU with caches, so I know what writing RTL is like. But the part I enjoyed most was trying to break it: writing a reference model, crafting corner-case stimulus, tracing a failing seed back to [a cache write-back hazard]. That's why my later projects were verification-focused, a UVM testbench for an AXI crossbar and CDC sign-off with JasperGold. I like that DV is where you find the bugs that would otherwise cost a respin, and having a design background helps me think like the designer when I'm hunting them.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Is your interest genuine and evidenced, or did you just apply to everything?
- Will you stay motivated in DV, or try to move to design immediately?
- 1point3acres: 'what related project did you do, what impact did it have, did you enjoy the output?'

### Pitfalls
- 'Design positions were full', 'DV is easier to get into', or 'it pays well'.
- Running down design or your previous major. The 1point3acres advice is: no complaining, but explain what you couldn't learn or impact there.
- Giving no example.

### Follow-ups
- **Would you want to move to design later?** Say you're open, but that DV skills compound and you see a long path in verification.
- **What's the hardest part of DV?** Knowing when you're done: coverage closure and plan completeness.
- **UVM or formal, which do you prefer?** Both. Simulation for breadth, formal for exhaustive proofs on control logic and CDC.

questions.title: Why should I hire you? (Why do you feel qualified for this job?)
questions.answer: 64 Toughest Q7: the most important question, because the interviewer must answer it to hire you. Walk through each requirement and follow it with why you meet it.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Walk through the role's top requirements and pair each with your proof, using the 64 Toughest's 'selling couplets'. Finish with something that sets you apart.

| Their need | Your proof |
| --- | --- |
| **SystemVerilog / UVM testbenches** | Built a full UVM env for an AXI4 2M×3S crossbar: agents, scoreboard, coverage; [N] tests, [X%] coverage. |
| **Protocol knowledge** | AXI4 channels, ordering and IDs, plus arbitration and decode, from the crossbar project. |
| **Formal / CDC** | JasperGold CDC sign-off on a 3-clock-domain NTT accelerator. |
| **Design intuition** | Built a 16-bit RISC CPU with caches, so I can read and reason about RTL. |
| **Differentiator** | I take a block from plan → testbench → closure on my own, and I document as I go. |

### Sample answer
> From the job description you need someone who can build and debug UVM testbenches, understands bus protocols, and can work with formal tools. I've built a UVM environment for an AXI4 crossbar end to end, closing [X%] functional coverage. I've done CDC sign-off with JasperGold on a three-clock-domain design. And because I also built a RISC CPU with caches, I can read RTL and talk to designers in their language. What I'd add is ownership: I'm used to taking a block from verification plan to coverage closure without needing much hand-holding.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Can you summarise your value against *their* needs?
- Confidence and preparation. If you stammer here, it's a red flag (64 Toughest).
- Whether you understand what the role actually requires.

### Pitfalls
- A generic answer ('I'm hard-working and passionate').
- Comparing yourself negatively with other candidates.
- Listing everything on your resume instead of matching their needs.

### Follow-ups
- **What's one area where you'd need to ramp up?** Name something real but learnable, e.g. emulation or their in-house flow, and how you'd ramp.
- **Why you over someone with industry experience?** Recent hands-on depth, learning speed, and your design + DV mix.

questions.title: Where do you see yourself in five years? (What is your long-range objective?)
questions.answer: 64 Toughest Q9: reassure them about long-term commitment; if you do excellent work, opportunities follow. 1point3acres #3/#15: focus on achievable objectives and what you're doing to reach them, e.g. 'the expert others rely upon'. Sugarac: growth in the role, more responsibility, mentoring.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Show ambition that fits inside this company's path: get excellent at the craft, own bigger scope, mentor others. Too specific sounds presumptuous; too vague sounds rudderless.

| Horizon | DV-flavoured answer |
| --- | --- |
| **1–2 years** | Become a strong contributor: own block-level testbenches, close coverage, debug fast. |
| **3–5 years** | Own verification of a larger subsystem: plan, methodology choices (UVM + formal), sign-off. |
| **Beyond title** | Be the person others ask about [interconnect / CDC / formal]; mentor new grads. |
| **What you're doing now** | Projects + learning [formal apps, emulation concepts, Python regression tooling]. |

### Sample answer
> In five years I'd like to be a verification engineer the team relies on for a whole subsystem: writing the plan, choosing where to use UVM versus formal, and driving it to sign-off. Short term, I want to get really good at the fundamentals here, owning block testbenches and closing coverage efficiently. I'd also like to become a go-to person for [interconnect or CDC] verification and help mentor newer engineers. I'm already building toward that with my AXI crossbar and JasperGold CDC work, and an internship here is the best next step.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Will you stay, or is this a stopover?
- Ambition level and self-direction.
- Do your goals line up with what the company can offer?

### Pitfalls
- 'In your seat' or naming specific promotions.
- Goals the company can't satisfy (switching fields, starting a company, moving to a city they don't have).
- 'I don't know.'

### Follow-ups
- **What are you doing now toward that?** Name concrete steps (courses, projects, tools).
- **Manager or technical track?** Technical depth first; open to leading later.
- **What if that path isn't available here?** Say you care about scope and learning more than titles.

questions.title: What are your short- and long-term goals, and what steps have you taken toward them?
questions.answer: 1point3acres #14: relate goals to the organisation; describe milestones and time periods. #73: show research and concrete steps (e.g. planned degree, certifications). 64 Toughest Q51: the trap is having no goals or only vague ones; describe milestones, timeline, why it matters, and the steps you're taking, concisely.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Have specific goals with milestones and a timeline, and evidence that you're already working on them. Relate them to this organisation.

| Piece | Example |
| --- | --- |
| **Short-term goal** | Finish thesis on [topic] by [date]; land a DV internship; master UVM RAL / SVA / formal apps. |
| **Steps taken** | Built AXI crossbar UVM TB; did JasperGold CDC sign-off; [reading UVM 1.2 spec / Verification Academy courses]. |
| **Long-term goal** | Become a subsystem-level DV owner / methodology expert. |
| **Milestones** | Year 1: own a block. Year 2–3: own a subsystem test plan. Year 5: lead verification of a major IP. |

### Sample answer
> My short-term goal is to finish my master's thesis on [topic] by [date] and start my career in design verification. This internship is a big part of that. To prepare, I built a full UVM testbench for an AXI crossbar, learned SVA and JasperGold for CDC sign-off, and I'm currently [working through UVM register-layer material / writing Python regression scripts]. Longer term, I want to own verification of a complex subsystem, from the plan through sign-off. My milestones are owning a block within my first year and a subsystem test plan within three.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Goal-setting habits. Many hiring managers are strong goal-setters and 'hire in kind' (64 Toughest).
- Specificity: milestones, time frames, actions.
- Alignment with the role.

### Pitfalls
- Vague goals ('grow as an engineer').
- Goals that the organisation can't support.
- Talking for more than 2 minutes.

### Follow-ups
- **Are you a goal-oriented person?** Yes, then give a past goal you set and met (see the 'set a goal and achieved it' question).
- **What will it take to reach them?** Name the skills, the mentorship and the scope you need, and show you'd seek them out.

questions.title: How do you define success, and how do you measure up to your own definition?
questions.answer: 64 Toughest Q58: 'success is the progressive realisation of a worthy goal', then summarise your achievements. 1point3acres #72: being good at something you love that helps others; balance. 1point3acres thread: define it as reaching self-set goals, then show your goals and future development.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Give a definition you actually use, such as 'progressive realisation of a worthy goal' or 'hitting the goals I set myself', then show your track record against it.

| Element | Example |
| --- | --- |
| **Definition** | Setting a meaningful goal and steadily reaching it, and in DV, shipping silicon with no escapes from the blocks I own. |
| **Goal set** | e.g. close [X%] functional + code coverage on AXI crossbar with zero open bugs by [date]. |
| **How I measured** | Coverage reports, bug tracker trend, a review by advisor. |
| **Result / next goal** | Met it [on time]; next goal: apply the same rigour at industry scale. |

### Sample answer
> For me, success is setting a meaningful goal and reaching it step by step, and then raising the bar. In verification terms, it means the blocks I sign off don't produce escapes. On my AXI crossbar project I set a goal of [X%] functional coverage with zero open bugs by [date], tracked it weekly with coverage reports, and met it [a week early]. I'd call that a success, but I'm not done. My next goal is to bring that same discipline to a production team, where the stakes and the scale are much higher.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Your values and what motivates you.
- Do you set goals for yourself? (1point3acres: 'success = reaching goals I set, so what are yours?')
- Evidence that you meet your own bar.

### Pitfalls
- Defining success only by money or title.
- A definition with no example of you meeting it.
- Sounding smug. 1point3acres suggests acknowledging that luck and the team played a part.

### Follow-ups
- **What's a time you weren't successful by that definition?** Bridge to your failure story.
- **How will you know this internship was a success?** Give concrete outcomes, e.g. delivered a TB component and found real bugs.

questions.title: Do you have any questions for me?
questions.answer: Sugarac: ask about room for improvement, the interviewer's proudest work, team engineering challenges, qualities they look for, day-to-day, and how many interns. Crack the BQ: onboarding, daily life, what they like about the company, next steps; show passion. 1point3acres resources: Work It Daily's 4C (connect, culture, challenges, close).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Always say yes. Ask 2–3 thoughtful questions that show you're interested and that you're already picturing yourself doing the job. Never ask nothing, and don't open with salary or vacation.

| Type (4C: connect, culture, challenges, close) | Example question |
| --- | --- |
| **Connect** | "What do you enjoy most about working on this team?" |
| **Culture** | "How do DV and design engineers collaborate here, e.g. when a bug is disputed?" |
| **Challenges** | "What are the biggest verification challenges the team faces right now: coverage closure, simulation time, formal adoption?" |
| **Close** | "What does success look like for an intern in the first 90 days?" / "What are the next steps?" |

### Sample answer
> Yes, a few. First, what does a typical week look like for a DV intern on this team, and what kind of block would I likely own? Second, what's the biggest verification challenge you're dealing with right now, for example simulation runtime, coverage closure, or where you use formal versus simulation? And finally, from your own experience, what distinguishes the interns who end up getting return offers?

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Genuine interest. 1point3acres reports a 'no hire' after a correct coding round because the candidate seemed uninterested.
- Preparation and curiosity.
- Your priorities, based on what you choose to ask.

### Pitfalls
- 'No, I think you covered everything.'
- Asking things you could Google.
- Asking about salary, PTO or remote work first.
- Asking for code feedback in a way that sounds needy. Sugarac's 'room for improvement in my code?' is OK if framed as wanting to learn.

### Follow-ups
- **(If they ask you back) What would you want to learn here?** Name one or two concrete technical areas.
- **Anything else?** 'What are the next steps in the process?'

questions.title: Describe your most challenging (or proudest) project.
questions.answer: Crack the BQ: what it is, what it's built with, the difficulty, how you overcame it, your contribution; draw diagrams. Make the 'challenge' credible: no one to ask, nobody had done it, few references. Sugarac example: a React bundle-size problem solved by reading source and rewriting a component. 64 Toughest Q49 (toughest challenge): pick a recent example that shows a quality key to the job. 1point3acres #74/#76: describe a success or accomplishment.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Explain what the project is (draw a picture if you can), why it was hard, what *you* did to overcome that, and the result. The challenge must be credibly hard, not just 'it was new to me'.

| STAR | Sample (DV scenario, adapt the [placeholders]) |
| --- | --- |
| **S**ituation | AXI4 2-master/3-slave crossbar; I built the UVM verification environment [alone / in a team of N]. |
| **T**ask | Verify arbitration, address decode, ID-based ordering and backpressure on 5 independent channels, with a scoreboard that handles out-of-order responses. |
| **A**ction | Designed an agent per port, a predictor that models the decode and arbitration, and an ID-indexed scoreboard. Few public references existed for multi-master scoreboarding, so I [read the AXI spec ordering rules, prototyped two scoreboard designs, asked my advisor to review]. Added constrained-random sequences + coverage crosses (master × slave × burst type × backpressure). |
| **R**esult | [N] tests, [X%] functional coverage, [Y] RTL bugs found, e.g. [a decode error on the boundary address]. Reused the agents in [another project]. |

### Sample answer
> My proudest project is a UVM testbench for an AXI4 crossbar with two masters and three slaves. The hard part was the scoreboard. With multiple masters, IDs and out-of-order responses, a simple in-order queue gives false mismatches. There wasn't much public material on this, so I worked from the AXI ordering rules, prototyped two scoreboard designs, and chose an ID-indexed predictor that models decode and arbitration. Then I wrote constrained-random sequences with coverage crosses over master, slave, burst type and backpressure. In the end I ran [N] tests, reached [X%] functional coverage and found [Y] RTL bugs, including [a decode error at a slave boundary address].

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Technical depth: can you explain it clearly and answer drill-downs?
- Your personal contribution versus the team's.
- Problem solving: self-learning, asking the right people, experimenting (Crack the BQ).

### Pitfalls
- A challenge that was easy to overcome ('it was new to me', 'I just Googled it'). The 1point3acres advice is to explain why help or references were scarce.
- Diving into detail before explaining what the thing is.
- Saying 'we' throughout so your role is invisible.

### Follow-ups
- **Draw the testbench architecture.** Sequencer → driver → DUT → monitor → predictor/scoreboard, plus coverage subscriber.
- **How did you know you were done?** Coverage goals from the verification plan + zero open bugs + regression stable over [N] seeds.
- **What would you do differently?** e.g. Write the plan earlier, add SVA protocol checkers on each interface, use RAL if registers exist.

questions.title: How did you prepare for this interview?
questions.answer: 1point3acres #8: found the posting, researched the website, mission and executives' bios, talked to friends in the industry, and 'I'm sure I'll find out a lot more in today's meetings.'
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Show methodical research into the company, role and team, and that you prepared technically too. This is a proxy for how you prepare for work.

| Area | What you did |
| --- | --- |
| **Company** | Read about recent products, [GTC talks / tech blog], and the JD in detail. |
| **People** | Talked to [a friend / alumnus] at the company; looked at the team's public papers/talks. |
| **Technical** | Reviewed UVM phases, SVA, CDC, AXI; re-ran my own projects to refresh details. |
| **Behavioral** | Prepared STAR stories mapped to the JD's skills. |

### Sample answer
> When I saw the posting I went through the JD line by line and mapped each requirement to something I've done. I read up on [the team's product area] and watched [a talk on GPU verification]. I also talked to [an NTHU alumnus who works in DV] about what the day-to-day looks like. On the technical side, I reviewed UVM, SVA and CDC fundamentals and went back over my AXI crossbar and CPU projects so I could explain every design decision. And I'm sure I'll learn a lot more from today's conversations.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Diligence and genuine interest.
- How you approach preparation in general.

### Pitfalls
- 'I didn't really prepare, I just came.'
- Saying you memorised answers.
- Over-claiming insider knowledge.

### Follow-ups
- **What did you learn that surprised you?** Have one specific fact.
- **What do you think this team does day-to-day?** Summarise it from the JD and ask them to confirm.

questions.title: 你是怎麼知道這個職位的？ (How did you hear about this position?)
questions.answer: 1point3acres BQ thread: answer truthfully (e.g. talked to the company's engineers at a career fair), then restate what the role does or needs and that you have done it, so you're a good fit.
questions.solution:
**重點：** 照實回答來源（career fair、內推、官網、教授），但重點在最後一句：「據我了解這個職位需要 X，而我做過 X，所以我是 good fit」。

| 步驟 | 內容 |
| --- | --- |
| **來源** | 例如：校園徵才 / 學長內推 / NVIDIA 官網 / LinkedIn。 |
| **你做了什麼** | 和該公司的 DV 工程師聊過，了解 team 在做 [interconnect / GPU block] 驗證。 |
| **你理解的職位** | 需要 SystemVerilog/UVM、protocol（AXI）、formal/CDC 經驗。 |
| **連結到你** | AXI crossbar UVM TB + JasperGold CDC sign-off → good fit。 |

### 範例回答 (Sample answer, English)
> I first saw it on [NVIDIA's careers page / at the NTHU career fair], and then I talked with [an alumnus who works in DV there] to learn more. From what I understand, the role is about building and debugging UVM testbenches for [interconnect / GPU] blocks, with some formal work. That's very close to what I've been doing, a UVM environment for an AXI4 crossbar and CDC sign-off with JasperGold, so it felt like a natural fit and I applied right away.

### 面試官在評估什麼 (What the interviewer is assessing)
- 是否誠實、是否主動（有沒有找人了解職位）。
- 你是否真的了解這個職位在做什麼。
- 1point3acres 原帖：關鍵是最後再重複一次「這個職位需要什麼，我做過，所以 good fit」。

### 常見陷阱 (Pitfalls)
- 只回答「網路上看到的」就停住，浪費一次推銷自己的機會。
- 編造內推人或過度誇大與員工的關係。
- 暗示自己海投、對哪家都無所謂。

### 追問 (Follow-ups)
- **Who referred you? (誰內推你？)** 照實回答，並簡短說明對方怎麼描述這個 team。
- **What attracted you in the JD? (JD 哪點吸引你？)** 挑 1–2 個和你專案最相關的關鍵字。

questions.title: Describe your ideal company, location and job.
questions.answer: 64 Toughest Q10: often a disguised 'overqualified' probe. Describe what this company offers, with specific sincere reasons; watch for the 'Avis complex'.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** The only right answer describes *this* opportunity: name the qualities this company and role offer and give a sincere reason why each one appeals to you.

| Dimension | Match to this company |
| --- | --- |
| **Company** | Engineering-driven, where verification is valued as a first-class discipline: [this company]. |
| **Team** | Strong mentors, code/plan reviews, a culture of learning: what you heard about this team. |
| **Work** | Verifying complex IP with modern methods: UVM, formal, emulation. |
| **Location** | Say that the location works for you (if true) with a real reason, e.g. [Hsinchu / Santa Clara] has the semiconductor ecosystem. |

### Sample answer
> My ideal job is one where verification is treated as an engineering discipline in its own right, with complex IP, modern methodology, and senior engineers who review your plans and code so you grow quickly. From what I've learned about this team, it does [interconnect verification with both UVM and formal] and has [a strong mentorship culture], which is exactly that. Location-wise, [Hsinchu / Santa Clara] is ideal for me because it's the centre of the semiconductor ecosystem.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Whether you'd actually be happy here, or are overqualified or looking elsewhere (64 Toughest).
- Whether you've researched the company.

### Pitfalls
- Describing a company that is obviously different (startup vs. huge corp, a different city).
- Making a smaller company feel 'second best' (the 'Avis complex').
- Being vague.

### Follow-ups
- **What would make you leave a job?** Lack of learning or ownership. Stay positive.
- **Big company or startup?** Explain why this company's size suits where you are in your career.

questions.title: What does it take to be successful as a design verification engineer? (What is the proper role of a good DV engineer?)
questions.answer: 64 Toughest Q37: identify 3–6 essential qualities for success in the role and commit them to memory; tailor to the hiring company's culture. 1point3acres #75: extra effort, attention to detail; success is continuous learning, not an end point.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Name 3–6 essential qualities of the role and show briefly that you have them. This tests whether you understand the job's place in the bigger picture.

| Quality | What it looks like |
| --- | --- |
| **Adversarial mindset** | Think about how to break the design, not prove it works. |
| **Planning & closure** | A verification plan tied to the spec; coverage-driven closure; know when you're done. |
| **Debug efficiency** | Waveforms, logs, reference models; narrow failures fast. |
| **Methodology breadth** | UVM simulation + SVA + formal + (later) emulation; pick the right tool. |
| **Communication** | Clear bug reports, spec clarifications with designers/architects; no blame. |
| **Continuous learning** | Protocols, tools, scripting (Python/Tcl) to automate regressions. |

### Sample answer
> I think a good DV engineer is the team's independent guarantee that the chip matches the spec. That takes a few things. First, an adversarial mindset: you're trying to break the design, not demonstrate it. Second, planning discipline, meaning a verification plan traced to the spec and coverage-driven closure so you know when you're done. Third, fast debug. Fourth, knowing when to use simulation, assertions or formal. And finally, communication, because a bug is only useful if the report is clear and the designer trusts you. I've tried to build each of these, for example [the plan-first approach and ID-based scoreboard in my AXI crossbar project].

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Whether you understand the profession beyond 'writes testbenches'.
- Maturity and big-picture thinking.

### Pitfalls
- A generic answer that would fit any job ('hard work').
- Listing tools only.
- No link back to your own behaviour.

### Follow-ups
- **Which of these is your weakest?** Answer honestly with a growth plan, e.g. emulation exposure.
- **How do you know verification is complete?** Plan items checked, coverage goals met, bug discovery rate flattened, reviews done.

questions.title: Describe a time when you had to handle a conflict at work. (How do you handle conflict?)
questions.answer: Big Interview sample: a schedule clash irritated a coworker; approach directly, explain, propose a new slot with an agenda, and learn the value of timely communication. 1point3acres #10: determine the source, discuss solutions, pick the best one; have a short story ready. Crack the BQ: the team goal comes first, use objective support before challenging someone, and keep personal grudges out.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Show a calm process: find the source of the conflict, focus on the shared goal, use data rather than opinions, agree on a solution, and say what you learned. Don't blame the other person.

| STAR | Sample (DV scenario, adapt the [placeholders]) |
| --- | --- |
| **S**ituation | In [course project / lab], a designer teammate and I disagreed on whether a failing check was an RTL bug or a testbench bug. It was blocking the regression the week before a milestone. |
| **T**ask | Resolve it quickly without damaging the working relationship, and get the regression green for the right reason. |
| **A**ction | Talked one-on-one instead of in the group chat; agreed the spec was the arbiter. Pulled up the waveform and the spec clause together, and wrote a minimal directed test that isolated the behaviour. It turned out the spec was ambiguous, so we asked [the advisor / spec owner] and documented the decision. |
| **R**esult | Fixed in [1 day]; we added an SVA for that rule so the disagreement couldn't recur. Our working relationship got better, and I learned to escalate ambiguous specs early instead of arguing about interpretation. |

### Sample answer
> In my [course project], a teammate who wrote the RTL and I disagreed about a failing check. He was sure it was a testbench bug and I thought it was the RTL, and it was blocking our regression right before a milestone. Instead of arguing in the group chat I asked to sit down with him, and we agreed to let the spec decide. We looked at the waveform and the spec clause together, and I wrote a small directed test that isolated the behaviour. It turned out the spec was ambiguous on [back-to-back write ordering], so we took it to [our advisor], documented the decision, and I added an assertion for that rule. We fixed it in a day. The main lesson for me was that most DV-versus-design conflicts are really spec ambiguities, and treating them that way takes the ego out of it.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Emotional maturity and professionalism.
- Whether you resolve conflict based on the team goal (Crack the BQ: 'everyone wants the work done well, so no conflict is unresolvable').
- Communication: direct, private, and backed by data.

### Pitfalls
- Making the other person the villain, or making yourself a pushover.
- A conflict that's trivial or purely personal.
- No resolution or lesson.
- 1point3acres: don't accuse others lightly, and don't blindly follow either. Show balanced judgement.

### Follow-ups
- **What if they still disagreed?** Escalate to the spec owner or lead with both views written down; commit to the decision.
- **Have you ever been wrong in a conflict?** Yes, then say what you learned (a good place for humility).
- **How do you prevent such conflicts?** Clarify the spec early, hold plan reviews with designers, and use assertions as executable spec.

questions.title: How have you handled a teammate who was not pulling their weight (a non-performing team member)?
questions.answer: 1point3acres #87: group discussed, asked for bare minimum, informed professor (not requesting action), split work, then asked to focus on 3 of 4 companies. 64 Toughest Q40: go directly to the person, persuade, then involve wider circles including your boss; never let it slide. 1point3acres thread: do you communicate proactively, share work for the team, and handle it professionally? Big Interview lists both peer and leader versions.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Talk to them directly and privately first, look for the cause, offer help, and re-scope if needed. Escalate transparently only if the team goal is at risk. Professional, not punitive.

| STAR | Sample (DV scenario, adapt the [placeholders]) |
| --- | --- |
| **S**ituation | In a [3-person course project], one teammate hadn't delivered the [monitor/scoreboard] two weeks before the demo. |
| **T**ask | Make sure the project shipped and get them back on track without poisoning the team. |
| **A**ction | Asked privately what was going on. They were [stuck on UVM TLM ports / overloaded with another course]. I paired with them for an hour on the analysis-port connection, split their task into smaller pieces with dates, and took one piece myself. When a deadline slipped again, I let our [TA / advisor] know the status factually: no complaints, just the plan. |
| **R**esult | They delivered the monitor; we demoed on time. I learned to check in early with milestones instead of waiting until the deadline. |

### Sample answer
> In a three-person course project, one teammate was responsible for the monitor and scoreboard, and two weeks before the demo there was almost nothing in the repo. I asked him privately what was going on. He was stuck on UVM analysis ports and also overloaded with another course. I paired with him for an hour to get the TLM connections working, then we split his work into smaller pieces with dates, and I took the coverage collector myself. When one date still slipped, I gave our TA a short factual status with the recovery plan, not a complaint. We demoed on time with everything working. The lesson I took away is to set small milestones early so problems show up while there's still time to help.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Do you communicate directly and professionally?
- Do you put the team result first, and are you willing to share work?
- Judgement on when and how to escalate. 64 Toughest: don't let it slide; widen the circle gradually.

### Pitfalls
- Complaining about or labelling the teammate as lazy.
- Silently doing all their work with no conversation (it hides the problem).
- Going to the professor or manager first without talking to the person.

### Follow-ups
- **What if they still didn't deliver?** Re-scope transparently with the lead and document ownership.
- **Did you agree with how the professor/manager handled it?** Stay respectful; explain your view and what you'd do next time.
- **How do you prevent this?** Clear owners, small milestones, early integration.

questions.title: Give an example of a time your team disagreed with your decision or idea. How did you manage it?
questions.answer: 1point3acres BQ thread (teammate disagrees with your view): did you make a quantitative comparison, prepare a detailed report or strong case, and communicate effectively?
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Back your position with quantitative evidence, listen to the objections seriously, look for a better combined option, and commit to the final decision even if it goes against you.

| STAR | Sample (DV scenario, adapt the [placeholders]) |
| --- | --- |
| **S**ituation | My team was choosing a scoreboard approach for the AXI crossbar TB: I proposed an ID-indexed predictor; teammates preferred a simpler in-order queue per slave. |
| **T**ask | Get the team to the technically right choice without forcing it through. |
| **A**ction | Instead of arguing, I built a [30-minute] prototype and ran both against a test with out-of-order responses: the in-order queue produced [N] false mismatches. I also acknowledged their concern (complexity) and proposed keeping the in-order path for single-ID traffic. |
| **R**esult | Team adopted the hybrid; zero false mismatches in [N] regressions. I learned that a small experiment beats a long debate. |

### Sample answer
> When we designed the scoreboard for our AXI crossbar testbench, I proposed an ID-indexed predictor, but my teammates preferred a simple in-order queue because it was easier to write. Rather than debate it, I spent half an hour prototyping both and ran them on a test with out-of-order responses. The in-order version produced [N] false mismatches. I also took their complexity concern seriously and suggested we keep the simple path for single-ID traffic and use the ID index only where ordering can differ. They agreed to the hybrid, and we had no false mismatches across [N] regressions. My takeaway was that a quick experiment settles a technical disagreement faster than any argument.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Can you influence without authority?
- 1point3acres: did you build a quantitative comparison or a strong case, and communicate it effectively?
- Are you open to being wrong, and do you commit once a decision is made?

### Pitfalls
- 'I was right and they eventually realised it.' That reads as arrogant.
- Caving immediately with no reasoning.
- Not mentioning what you learned from their objections.

### Follow-ups
- **What if the data had favoured them?** Say you'd switch and credit them; the goal is the right answer.
- **Tell me about a time you were overruled.** Show that you disagreed and then committed fully.

questions.title: How have you handled personality clashes or someone who was difficult to work with?
questions.answer: 1point3acres #9: difficulty only with people dishonest about work; talked to a colleague who took credit, and her behaviour changed. Lesson: perceptions aren't always right, so check. 1point3acres resources: 'work with someone who was difficult to get along with'.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Separate the person from the problem. Try to understand their perspective, adapt how you communicate, keep the focus on shared work, and show that the relationship improved.

| STAR | Sample (DV scenario, adapt the [placeholders]) |
| --- | --- |
| **S**ituation | A lab-mate on a shared [FPGA board / server licence] was very blunt and often dismissed suggestions in meetings. |
| **T**ask | We had to co-own [the regression setup] for [N] weeks. |
| **A**ction | Asked for a 1:1 coffee to understand how they liked to work: they preferred written, concrete proposals over brainstorming. Switched to short written proposals with data; credited their ideas publicly; kept discussions about the work. |
| **R**esult | Collaboration became smooth; they ended up [reviewing my scripts / co-authoring X]. Learned that 'difficult' often means 'different working style'. |

### Sample answer
> In my lab I shared ownership of [the regression scripts and server queue] with a labmate who was very blunt and often shot down ideas in meetings, which frustrated people. I asked him for a coffee to understand how he liked to work, and it turned out he disliked open-ended brainstorming but responded well to concrete, written proposals with data. So I started sending a short write-up before each discussion, and I made a point of crediting his ideas in group meetings. Things got much smoother, and he ended up reviewing my regression scripts and catching [a seed-handling bug]. I learned that someone who seems difficult often just has a different working style, and that it's worth asking before judging.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Interpersonal maturity; can you work with anyone?
- Empathy and adaptability.
- 1point3acres #9: the only acceptable 'difficult' traits are things like dishonesty, never personality types.

### Pitfalls
- Bad-mouthing the person or using labels like 'personality clash' (64 Toughest warns against them).
- Saying 'I get along with everyone' with no example.
- A story where you never changed anything about your own behaviour.

### Follow-ups
- **What kinds of people do you find hard to work with?** People who aren't honest about the status of their work. Then give the story of addressing it calmly.
- **What if they never changed?** Keep it professional, focus on deliverables, and involve the lead if work suffers.

questions.title: Can you share an instance where you went over and above to help a team member?
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Pick help that cost you real effort, was driven by the team goal, and had a measurable effect for them and the project. Don't make it sound like you rescued someone who was incompetent.

| STAR | Sample (DV scenario, adapt the [placeholders]) |
| --- | --- |
| **S**ituation | A teammate new to SystemVerilog was struggling to get their [AXI slave BFM] working before integration. |
| **T**ask | My own tasks were on track; the integration date was at risk. |
| **A**ction | Spent two evenings pairing with them: walked through clocking blocks and race-free driving, shared my [driver template] and a debug checklist (waveform first, then log). Let them write the code; I reviewed. |
| **R**esult | Integration happened on schedule; they later [wrote the response-reordering sequence on their own]. I turned the checklist into a team wiki page. |

### Sample answer
> Before our integration milestone, a teammate who was new to SystemVerilog couldn't get his AXI slave BFM to drive correctly. Signals were changing on the wrong edge. My own tasks were on track, so I spent two evenings pairing with him. I explained clocking blocks and why driving from a clocking block avoids races, shared my driver template, and walked him through my debug order, waveform first and then logs. I made a point of letting him write the code while I reviewed. We integrated on schedule, and he later wrote the out-of-order response sequence completely on his own. I also turned the checklist into a page on our team wiki, so the next person had it too.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Team orientation and generosity.
- Whether you teach rather than just take over.

### Pitfalls
- Implying you sacrificed your own deliverables irresponsibly.
- A story with no real effort ('I answered a question').
- Making the teammate look bad.

### Follow-ups
- **How did you balance it with your own work?** Say your work was on track first, and give a time box.
- **What did you learn from teaching?** Explaining the concept deepened your own understanding of clocking and races.

questions.title: Tell me about a time when you or your team achieved a significant goal.
questions.answer: Big Interview sample (hospital admin): reduce surgery wait from 12 to 8 weeks by analysing each step and streamlining; worked for months, hit the goal and improved satisfaction.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Give an ambitious, measurable goal, the plan, your specific role, and the quantified result. Credit the team while making your own contribution clear.

| STAR | Sample (DV scenario, adapt the [placeholders]) |
| --- | --- |
| **S**ituation | Our [course / lab] team had to tape out / demo [the NTT accelerator] with 3 clock domains by [date]. |
| **T**ask | My role: verification lead for CDC and the top-level testbench. Goal: zero CDC violations and [X%] coverage before freeze. |
| **A**ction | Set up JasperGold CDC early, triaged [N] initial violations into real vs. waivable, worked with the designer to add [2-flop synchronisers / async FIFO] where needed, wrote waivers with justification; tracked coverage weekly. |
| **R**esult | Clean CDC sign-off [N days] before freeze; [X%] functional coverage; [demo/tape-out] succeeded. Team result plus my contribution clearly stated. |

### Sample answer
> In my NTT accelerator project, our team had to deliver a design with three clock domains by [date], and I owned CDC and top-level verification. The goal was zero unwaived CDC violations and [X%] functional coverage before the freeze. I set up JasperGold CDC early instead of at the end. The first run reported [N] violations, which I sorted into real crossings and ones that were structurally safe. For the real ones I worked with the designer to add proper synchronisers and [an async FIFO]. For the rest I wrote waivers with written justifications that our advisor reviewed. We reached a clean sign-off [N days] early and hit our coverage goal. Starting CDC early was the decision that made the difference.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Goal orientation and planning.
- Collaboration, and your specific contribution within the team.

### Pitfalls
- Only 'we' with no 'I'.
- A goal with no measurable outcome.
- Taking credit for the whole team's work.

### Follow-ups
- **What was the biggest obstacle?** Triaging the initial flood of CDC violations, solved by categorising them.
- **How did you decide what to waive?** Quasi-static signals or properly synchronised paths with documented reasoning, reviewed by a second person.

questions.title: Share an example of when you had to adapt to a team member's working style.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Show that you noticed a different style, adapted without resentment, and that it improved results. Flexibility is the skill being tested.

| STAR | Sample (DV scenario, adapt the [placeholders]) |
| --- | --- |
| **S**ituation | Worked with a designer who preferred long uninterrupted coding blocks and disliked frequent pings; I liked quick iterative syncs. |
| **T**ask | Needed frequent RTL drops to keep the testbench moving. |
| **A**ction | Agreed on a fixed daily drop time + a shared bug list instead of ad-hoc messages; batched my questions; used the tracker comments for async discussion. |
| **R**esult | Fewer interruptions for them, predictable drops for me; bug turnaround went from [X] to [Y] days. |

### Sample answer
> On one project the designer I worked with liked long, uninterrupted blocks of focused time, while I was used to quick back-and-forth messages whenever I found something. I could tell my pings were frustrating him. So I suggested a fixed daily RTL drop time and a shared bug list, batched my questions, and moved most discussion into comments on the tracker. He got his focus time and I got predictable drops. Our bug turnaround went from about [X] days to [Y]. It taught me to ask people early how they prefer to collaborate instead of assuming my style works for everyone.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Flexibility and empathy.
- Whether you see collaboration as something you design deliberately.

### Pitfalls
- Framing the other style as wrong.
- Adapting so much that the work suffered.

### Follow-ups
- **What's your own preferred working style?** Be honest and show that it's flexible.
- **Have you had a teammate adapt to you?** Yes, e.g. when you learned to write things down for someone who prefers async communication.

questions.title: Talk about a time when you had to motivate a demotivated team member.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Find out *why* they lost motivation (overwhelm, unclear purpose, no wins), address that cause, help them get a small win, and recognise their progress.

| STAR | Sample (DV scenario, adapt the [placeholders]) |
| --- | --- |
| **S**ituation | Mid-semester, a teammate stopped contributing after their coverage model kept getting [low numbers] and the reviewer criticised it. |
| **T**ask | Keep them engaged; we needed their part for the final report. |
| **A**ction | Talked privately: they felt the work was invisible and they were stuck. Broke the coverage closure into small goals, showed them how to read the uncovered bins report, suggested two targeted sequences. Highlighted their improvement in the next team meeting. |
| **R**esult | Coverage went from [X%] to [Y%] in a week; they took ownership of the coverage section of the report. |

### Sample answer
> Mid-semester, one of my teammates went quiet after her coverage model got harsh review comments and the numbers were stuck at [X%]. I asked her privately how things were going. She felt stuck and thought her work wasn't valued. We sat down with the uncovered-bins report together, and I showed her how to turn each hole into a targeted sequence, then we split the closure into small daily goals. When she reached [Y%] a week later, I made sure to call that out in our team meeting. She took ownership of the whole coverage chapter in our final report. I learned that motivation usually comes back once someone has a small win and feels their work is seen.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Empathy and leadership without authority.
- Whether you diagnose before you act.

### Pitfalls
- Pep-talk only ('I told her to cheer up').
- Taking the work away from them.
- Talking about the person condescendingly.

### Follow-ups
- **What if the cause had been personal?** Respect their privacy, offer flexibility, and adjust the plan with the lead.
- **How do you keep yourself motivated?** Small milestones and visible progress, e.g. a coverage trend chart.

questions.title: Are you a team player? Describe a teamwork experience, your role, and the team's result.
questions.answer: 1point3acres #4: give behavioural examples; emphasise openness to diversity and the team above the individual; likely leads to conflict questions. #77: rower example (act as one) plus team leader ensuring equal contribution. Sugarac: internship teamwork, extensive communication, optimisation, 30% improvement.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Don't just say 'yes'. Prove it with a story: the team's goal, your specific role, how you communicated and coordinated, and the shared result.

| STAR | Sample (DV scenario, adapt the [placeholders]) |
| --- | --- |
| **S**ituation | A [3-person] team verifying the 16-bit RISC CPU with caches for [course]. |
| **T**ask | My role: memory-subsystem verification (cache + memory model) while others did ISA tests and RTL. |
| **A**ction | Held a 15-min weekly sync; shared a common transaction class so everyone's checkers spoke the same language; reviewed each other's tests; when the ISA tester got blocked by a cache bug, I prioritised reproducing it with a minimal test. |
| **R**esult | All [N] ISA tests + [M] cache stress tests passed; we found [Y] bugs, including [a write-back/eviction hazard]. Grade [/ demo] [result]. |

### Sample answer
> Yes. A good example is our 16-bit RISC CPU project, a team of three. I owned verification of the memory subsystem, the caches and the memory model, while my teammates did the ISA tests and the RTL. I set up a short weekly sync and proposed a shared transaction class so all our checkers used the same format, which made combining results easy. When a teammate's ISA tests were blocked by what looked like a cache bug, I dropped my current task and wrote a minimal reproducer. It turned out to be [a write-back during eviction hazard]. In the end everything passed: [N] ISA tests and [M] cache stress tests. For me, being a team player means unblocking other people before I polish my own part.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Team orientation backed by evidence (1point3acres: 'almost everyone says yes').
- Openness to different backgrounds; putting the team above the individual.
- Often a lead-in to conflict questions, so be ready for them.

### Pitfalls
- A plain 'yes' with no example.
- Bragging. 1point3acres: say it in a matter-of-fact tone.
- Not being able to say what your role was.

### Follow-ups
- **Describe a conflict in that team.** Have the conflict STAR ready.
- **What's your ideal working environment?** Clear ownership, frequent integration, and open debate based on data.

questions.title: Tell me about a time you disagreed with your manager or someone in authority. (What would you say if your boss loved an idea you thought was bad?)
questions.answer: 64 Toughest Q38: emphasise the positive first, raise reservations specifically and objectively, try to make the idea stronger; if overruled, give full support. Integrity first. 1point3acres resources: conflict with someone in authority.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Choose honesty, delivered constructively. Start from what's good about the idea, raise specific factual concerns, offer an improvement, and if you're overruled, support the decision fully.

| STAR | Sample (DV scenario, adapt the [placeholders]) |
| --- | --- |
| **S**ituation | My advisor wanted to skip formal CDC and rely on gate-level simulation for the 3-clock NTT accelerator to save time. |
| **T**ask | I believed simulation would miss metastability-related bugs; needed to raise this respectfully. |
| **A**ction | Acknowledged the schedule concern; prepared a one-page comparison: what simulation can/can't catch on CDC, an example of a missing synchroniser that sims passed, and an estimate that JasperGold CDC setup would take [2 days]. Proposed doing it in parallel with sims. |
| **R**esult | Advisor agreed; CDC found [N] real issues sims missed. Had they said no, I'd have run sims fully and noted the risk in the report. |

### Sample answer
> My advisor once suggested we skip formal CDC analysis on our three-clock NTT accelerator and rely on simulation to save time. I understood the schedule pressure, but I knew simulation can't really show metastability problems. So I wrote a one-page comparison of what simulation catches and what it misses on clock crossings, with an example of an unsynchronised path that passed every sim, and an estimate that JasperGold CDC setup would take about two days in parallel with our simulations. He agreed, and the CDC run found [N] real issues the sims had missed. If he'd said no, I would have committed to the simulation plan and documented the risk, but I think he appreciated getting the data instead of just an opinion.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Integrity versus loyalty. 64 Toughest: honesty is the most important thing you owe your boss.
- Whether you can disagree respectfully and with data.
- Whether you commit once you're overruled.

### Pitfalls
- Sounding insubordinate or bitter.
- Never disagreeing ('I always follow instructions').
- Disagreeing in public or going around your manager.

### Follow-ups
- **What if they still said no?** Say you'd support the decision fully and record the risk.
- **Tell me about a time you were overruled and the decision turned out right.** Show humility and what you learned.

questions.title: Describe a situation in which you had to arrive at a compromise or guide others to a compromise.
questions.answer: 1point3acres #88: disagreement with a professor's grading of an opinion question; both agreed to adjust; compromise is the key to problem resolution.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Find each side's underlying interest, propose an option that satisfies the critical ones, and make the trade-off explicit so everyone can accept it.

| STAR | Sample (DV scenario, adapt the [placeholders]) |
| --- | --- |
| **S**ituation | Our team had limited simulator licence time: I wanted long random regressions; a teammate wanted licences for gate-level sims before the deadline. |
| **T**ask | Both needs were legitimate; we couldn't do both fully. |
| **A**ction | Listed each side's must-haves: I needed [N] seeds on the new arbiter; they needed GLS on [2] key tests. Proposed: nightly random regression with fewer seeds + daytime GLS slots; prioritised seeds on changed blocks. |
| **R**esult | Both goals met; regression still caught [a bug] in the arbiter; GLS passed. Learned to negotiate on interests, not positions. |

### Sample answer
> Before a deadline, our team had limited simulator licences. I wanted long random regressions on the new arbiter, while a teammate needed licences for gate-level simulation. Rather than argue about who got them, we each listed our must-haves. I really needed about [N] seeds focused on the changed arbiter, not the whole suite, and he needed two key GLS tests run daily. So we ran a trimmed, targeted random regression overnight and gave him the daytime slots for GLS. Both goals were met, and the overnight run still caught [a starvation bug in the arbiter]. What I took from it is that compromise gets easier once you separate what people are asking for from what they actually need.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Negotiation and collaboration skills.
- Ability to see the other side's point of view.

### Pitfalls
- A 'compromise' where you simply won.
- Splitting the difference in a way that hurt quality.
- Picking a combative story, like the 1point3acres sample of arguing with a professor about political opinions.

### Follow-ups
- **When should you not compromise?** On sign-off quality or integrity, e.g. waiving a real CDC bug.
- **How did you get buy-in?** By making the trade-off explicit and agreeing on a fallback.

questions.title: How have you worked with a diverse or multidisciplinary group? (Convince me you can adapt to a wide variety of people and situations.)
questions.answer: 1point3acres resources: Flexibility ('adapt to a wide variety of people, situations and environments') and Teamwork ('contribute to a multi-disciplinary team').
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Show that you adjust vocabulary, channel and level of detail to different backgrounds, find common ground in the shared goal, and that the diversity improved the result.

| STAR | Sample (DV scenario, adapt the [placeholders]) |
| --- | --- |
| **S**ituation | The NTT accelerator project combined [crypto/algorithm students], RTL designers, and me (verification); some members were [international / from other departments]. |
| **T**ask | Turn an algorithm spec into verifiable hardware behaviour; everyone spoke a different 'language'. |
| **A**ction | Asked the algorithm folks for a Python golden model and used it as my reference model; translated hardware constraints (latency, bit widths) into plain terms for them; ran meetings in English with written summaries for non-native speakers. |
| **R**esult | Reference-model-based checking found [N] mismatches in modular reduction; the team shipped on time. Learned that a shared executable model is a great common language. |

### Sample answer
> My NTT accelerator project brought together people from very different backgrounds: algorithm people from [the crypto lab], RTL designers, and me on verification, with [members from several countries]. The algorithm side thought in polynomials and the hardware side in cycles and bit widths. I asked the algorithm team for a Python golden model and used it directly as my scoreboard's reference, so we had one shared source of truth. I also explained hardware constraints like latency and fixed-point widths in plain terms, and sent written summaries after meetings for people who preferred reading in English. That reference model caught [N] mismatches in modular reduction early. The lesson: give a diverse team one executable artefact everyone can point to.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Adaptability and communication across backgrounds.
- Whether you treat diversity as a strength.

### Pitfalls
- Patronising language about other cultures or disciplines.
- No concrete adaptation you made yourself.

### Follow-ups
- **How do you explain DV to a non-engineer?** 'We're the people who try to break the chip before the customer does.'
- **Tell me about a misunderstanding caused by different backgrounds.** Name one and what you changed afterwards.

questions.title: Tell me about a time when you mentored or coached someone.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Show that you diagnosed what the person needed, taught them to do it themselves rather than doing it for them, checked progress, and that they became independent.

| STAR | Sample (DV scenario, adapt the [placeholders]) |
| --- | --- |
| **S**ituation | A junior lab member / new student had to verify a [FIFO / UART] for their first project and had never used UVM. |
| **T**ask | Help them become productive in [3 weeks] without doing it for them. |
| **A**ction | Gave them a minimal working UVM skeleton, explained the flow (sequence → driver → DUT → monitor → scoreboard) with a diagram, set weekly goals (agent → scoreboard → coverage), and did code reviews with questions rather than answers. |
| **R**esult | They delivered a working environment with [X%] coverage; later onboarded the next junior using the same material. |

### Sample answer
> Last year a junior student in our lab had to verify [an async FIFO] and had never used UVM. Instead of handing over my code, I gave him a minimal working skeleton and drew the flow from sequence to driver to DUT to monitor to scoreboard. We set weekly goals: first a working agent, then the scoreboard, then coverage. In code reviews I asked questions like 'what happens if read and write hit the same cycle?' rather than pointing out the fix. In about [four weeks] he had a working environment at [X%] coverage, and later he used the same material to onboard the next new student. It also made me much better at explaining why UVM is structured the way it is.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Leadership and teaching ability.
- Patience; whether you build others' independence.

### Pitfalls
- Doing the work for them.
- Sounding condescending.

### Follow-ups
- **How do you adapt to different learners?** Some want the big picture first and some want a working example first, so ask.
- **What did you learn from mentoring?** Teaching exposed gaps in your own understanding, e.g. phasing or objections.

questions.title: 團隊因為不熟悉新技術而遇到困難、失去動力時，你怎麼做？ (Describe a time you had to use a technology you didn't know well, or your team struggled with one.)
questions.answer: Sugarac (中文): 團隊因不熟悉新技術失去動力，帶大家重新規劃、重新定義 core feature，自己快速學習嘗試，與隊友分享；失敗很多（錯的 library/API/框架），強調 fix fast 與取捨；帶領隊友 list problems、規劃時間、設定 milestone。1point3acres resources: 'Describe a time where you were required to use a certain technology that you did not know well.'
questions.solution:
**重點：** 先交代團隊的困境，再展現：重新規劃與定義核心範圍（project management）、自己快速學習並試錯（move fast）、把學到的分享給隊友（teamwork）、設定 milestone 帶領團隊；最後講結果與學到的經驗。

| STAR | 範例情境 (DV scenario，請替換 [placeholders]) |
| --- | --- |
| **S**ituation | 專案需要用 JasperGold 做 CDC sign-off（或第一次用 UVM），團隊沒人用過，進度停滯、士氣低落。 |
| **T**ask | 在 [N 週] 內完成三個 clock domain 的 CDC 驗證，同時把團隊拉回正軌。 |
| **A**ction | 1) 重新定義核心範圍：先只做 CDC structural check，再做 functional（protocol）check；2) 我先花 [2 天] 讀 tool 文件與跑官方範例，踩過錯誤的 constraint / clock 定義，強調 fail fast、fix fast；3) 寫一頁 cheat sheet、帶隊友跑第一次；4) 列出問題清單、訂 milestone，每週檢查。 |
| **R**esult | 準時完成 sign-off，抓到 [N] 個真正的 synchronizer 問題；隊友能獨立跑 tool。下次面對新工具會更快上手。 |

### 範例回答 (Sample answer, English)
> On my NTT accelerator project we had to do CDC sign-off with JasperGold, and nobody on the team had used it. Progress stalled and people were getting discouraged. I suggested we re-plan: do the structural CDC checks first and treat the protocol-level checks as a second milestone. I spent two days working through the tool documentation and examples. I made mistakes along the way, like wrong clock-group definitions, but I fixed them quickly and wrote a one-page cheat sheet. Then I walked each teammate through their first run, and we tracked open issues against weekly milestones. We finished sign-off on time and found [N] real synchroniser problems, and now everyone can run the tool on their own.

### 面試官在評估什麼 (What the interviewer is assessing)
- 學習能力與 move fast：能否在資源少的情況下快速上手。
- Leadership：能否在團隊失去動力時重新規劃、設定 milestone。
- Teamwork：是否把知識分享出去，而不是只有自己會。

### 常見陷阱 (Pitfalls)
- 只說「我上網查了就會了」——太容易，不構成 challenge（Crack the BQ 提醒要說明為什麼沒人可問、資料少）。
- 把隊友描述得很無能。
- 沒有具體 milestone 或結果。

### 追問 (Follow-ups)
- **How do you learn a new EDA tool quickly? (如何快速學新 tool？)** 官方範例 → 最小可行案例 → 套到自己的 design → 記錄 cheat sheet。
- **What mistakes did you make? (你犯了什麼錯？)** 例如 clock 定義錯導致大量 false violation，學會先驗證 setup。

questions.title: Tell me about a time when you solved a complex problem. (What major problem have you dealt with recently?)
questions.answer: Big Interview sample (accountant): consolidating financial data after acquisitions; revamped processes and added a QA review. 1point3acres #80; resources: 'Describe a time when you solved a problem and how you came up with the solution'; 'put your technical expertise to use to solve a problem'.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Explain why the problem was complex: several interacting causes, intermittent behaviour, unclear ownership. Then show a structured approach: reproduce, isolate, form hypotheses, verify, fix, prevent.

| STAR | Sample (DV scenario, adapt the [placeholders]) |
| --- | --- |
| **S**ituation | The 3-clock-domain NTT accelerator produced wrong results [~1 in N] runs at the top level, but every block-level test passed. |
| **T**ask | Find the root cause before the [demo / freeze] in [N days]. |
| **A**ction | 1) Made it reproducible: logged seeds and found it correlated with clock-ratio settings. 2) Isolated: bypassed blocks one by one using the Python golden model as the reference at each boundary. 3) Hypothesis: a multi-bit control bus crossing domains without a proper handshake. 4) Confirmed with JasperGold CDC (flagged that path) and a targeted sim with skewed clocks. 5) Fixed with a req/ack handshake; added an assertion + CDC rule to the sign-off checklist. |
| **R**esult | Failure rate went to 0 over [N] seeds × [M] clock ratios. Root-cause write-up became part of the team's CDC checklist. |

### Sample answer
> On my NTT accelerator, the top-level simulation produced wrong results in roughly one run in [N], even though every block-level test passed. It was complex because there were three clock domains and the failure was intermittent. First I made it reproducible by logging seeds and noticed it correlated with certain clock-frequency ratios. Then I isolated it by comparing each block boundary against our Python golden model, which narrowed it down to the interface between two domains. My hypothesis was a multi-bit control bus crossing without a handshake. JasperGold CDC confirmed it, and a sim with skewed clocks reproduced it every time. We replaced the crossing with a request/acknowledge handshake and I added an assertion for it. After that we saw zero failures across [N] seeds and all clock ratios, and the root-cause write-up became part of our CDC checklist.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Structured problem solving under ambiguity.
- Technical depth in the details.
- Whether you prevent the problem from coming back, not just fix it.

### Pitfalls
- A problem that isn't actually complex.
- Skipping the reasoning and jumping straight to the fix.
- Taking credit for a team discovery.

### Follow-ups
- **How did you know it was CDC and not a logic bug?** Clock-ratio correlation, block tests passing, and the CDC tool flag plus a deterministic reproduction with skewed clocks.
- **Why not just add a 2-flop synchroniser?** Multi-bit buses can be sampled incoherently. You need a handshake, Gray code, or an async FIFO.
- **What would you automate next time?** A clock-ratio sweep in the regression and a CDC check in CI.

questions.title: Can you share an instance where your initial solution to a problem didn't work? What did you do?
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Admit that the first approach failed, show how you noticed quickly, what you learned about the problem from the failure, and how the second approach succeeded.

| STAR | Sample (DV scenario, adapt the [placeholders]) |
| --- | --- |
| **S**ituation | Coverage for the AXI crossbar was stuck at [X%]: specific cross bins (both masters → same slave with max backpressure) never hit. |
| **T**ask | Close the holes before sign-off. |
| **A**ction | First try: increased the number of random seeds to [N×]. Coverage barely moved, so pure randomness was the wrong tool. Analysed the bins, wrote a virtual sequence coordinating both masters plus a slave-side backpressure knob, and constrained timing windows. |
| **R**esult | Holes closed in [1 day]; the new sequence also exposed [an arbitration fairness bug]. Lesson: when coverage plateaus, change the stimulus, don't just add seeds. |

### Sample answer
> When I was closing coverage on my AXI crossbar testbench, I got stuck at [X%]. The missing bins were both masters hitting the same slave under heavy backpressure. My first fix was to run [ten times] more random seeds. After a day, coverage had barely moved, and that told me something: the scenario was too unlikely for independent random masters. So I wrote a virtual sequence that coordinated both masters onto the same slave and added a backpressure knob on the slave side. The holes closed within a day, and the new sequence exposed [an arbitration fairness bug] that random testing had never reached. What I learned is that a coverage plateau is a signal to change the stimulus, not to throw more compute at it.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Resilience and adaptability.
- Learning from failed attempts rather than repeating them.

### Pitfalls
- Never admitting a first attempt failed.
- Blaming the tool or the environment.
- Persisting too long with an approach that clearly wasn't working.

### Follow-ups
- **How long did you persist with the first approach?** Give a short time box, and the data that told you to switch.
- **When is more seeds the right answer?** When bins are reachable but simply rare and coverage is still climbing.

questions.title: Tell me about a time you failed. (Give an example of a decision you made that was a failure.)
questions.answer: Big Interview sample (HR): chose an ATS that wasn't user-friendly, admitted the bad decision, picked another with a colleague, +20% efficiency; learned a holistic approach. Sugarac: miscommunication about the point person while the supervisor travelled; now clarifies weekly. 1point3acres #12: pick a minor incident from a while back that taught a valuable lesson.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Pick a real but non-catastrophic failure that you owned. Spend most of the time on what you did to recover and what you now do differently, ideally with evidence you applied the lesson later.

| STAR | Sample (DV scenario, adapt the [placeholders]) |
| --- | --- |
| **S**ituation | On the RISC CPU project I decided to build the testbench around directed tests only, to save time. |
| **T**ask | Verify the cache + pipeline before the course demo. |
| **A**ction | All directed tests passed, but during the demo the professor ran a program that triggered a [load-use hazard during a cache miss], and the CPU hung. I owned it in front of the class, reproduced it that evening, and added a constrained-random instruction generator plus a reference ISS comparison. |
| **R**esult | Random testing found [N] more bugs within a week. Since then every project I do has random stimulus + a reference model from day one, as in the AXI crossbar TB. |

### Sample answer
> On my RISC CPU project I decided to verify with directed tests only, because I thought random stimulus would take too long to set up. All [N] directed tests passed. Then during the demo the professor ran his own program, which triggered [a load-use hazard during a cache miss], and the CPU hung. That was my decision and I owned it. That evening I reproduced the bug, then built a constrained-random instruction generator that compared against a simple instruction-set model. Within a week it found [N] more bugs. Since then, every project I do has random stimulus and a reference model from day one, which is exactly how I built my AXI crossbar testbench.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Accountability: do you own it, or blame others?
- Learning and growth, with evidence you applied the lesson.
- 1point3acres #12: employers care about your ability to cope and learn, not about perfection.

### Pitfalls
- 'I've never really failed.'
- A disaster that raises doubts about your judgement for this job.
