| **Habit now** | I always run smoke regression before pushing, and I review my day's changes before leaving. |

### Sample answer
> Nothing major comes to mind, but there's one small thing early in my master's I'm not proud of. I pushed a testbench change without running the regression because I was in a hurry, and it broke a teammate's tests for most of a day. I apologised and fixed it right away. Since then I never push without the smoke regression, and at the end of each day I quickly look back over what I changed and who it might affect. That habit has saved me more than once.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- How you think on your feet (64 Toughest).
- Whether you overshare or show poor judgement.

### Pitfalls
- Confessing personal or family regrets. The 64 Toughest calls these 'disastrous'.
- Something ethically serious.
- Stonewalling with a flat 'nothing' and no follow-up.

### Follow-ups
- **Anything more serious?** Stay with small, learned-from examples, and stay calm.
- **How do you make amends when you've let a teammate down?** Own it quickly, fix it, and prevent it from happening again.

questions.title: Why are you leaving (or did you leave) your current position? (Why do you want to switch?)
questions.answer: 64 Toughest Q5: never badmouth; best reasons are more opportunity, responsibility, growth (or money). If fired, describe it candidly from the company's viewpoint without bitterness. Sugarac: 'Why do you want to switch jobs?'
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Never be negative about your past employer, lab or school. Give a positive reason that points toward this opportunity: growth, scope, learning, a better fit with your goals.

| Situation | Positive framing |
| --- | --- |
| **Student version** | "I'm finishing my master's and want industry-scale verification experience." |
| **Job-switch version** | "I've learned a lot at X; I'm looking for [deeper DV ownership / larger designs] which this role offers." |
| **If let go** | State it briefly and honestly from the company's point of view, without bitterness. |
| **Bridge** | Connect to what this role offers. |

### Sample answer
> I've learned a lot in my master's lab, especially building verification environments end to end. But a university project can only go so far: the designs are smaller, and there's no production sign-off or emulation. I'm looking for verification at real industrial scale, with senior engineers to learn from, and this internship offers exactly that.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Whether you're running from something (a red flag) or toward something.
- Your loyalty and professionalism.

### Pitfalls
- Bad-mouthing your boss, lab, advisor or company. 'Any mud you hurl will only soil your suit' (64 Toughest).
- Words like 'personality clash' or 'didn't get along'.
- Lying about having been fired. It's unethical and easy to check.

### Follow-ups
- **What would make you stay at your current place?** Be honest, but put the emphasis on growth.
- **Were you let go?** Answer truthfully and briefly, with no bitterness and a forward focus.

questions.title: The "Silent Treatment": the interviewer just stares at you in silence after your answer. What do you do?
questions.answer: 64 Toughest Q6: unprepared candidates ramble; instead, keep quiet a while and then ask politely, 'Is there anything else I can fill in on that point?'
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Don't fill the silence by rambling. Wait calmly, then ask politely: "Is there anything else I can fill in on that point?"

| Step | What to say |
| --- | --- |
| **Recognise it** | A stress test, not a sign that you said something wrong. |
| **Hold** | Stay composed and keep a friendly expression for a few seconds. |
| **Ask** | "Is there anything else I can clarify on that point?" |
| **Don't** | Don't backtrack, add unprompted weaknesses, or contradict yourself. |

### Sample answer
> (after a pause, calmly) "Is there anything else I can clarify on that, maybe more detail on how I set up the scoreboard?"

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Composure under stress.
- Whether you talk yourself out of a job.

### Pitfalls
- Rambling and adding damaging information.
- Changing your answer just because of the silence.
- Looking visibly flustered.

### Follow-ups
- **(In technical interviews) What if they're silent while you code?** Narrate your thinking briefly. Silence often just means they're taking notes.
- **What if they still say nothing?** Offer to move on: 'Happy to go deeper there or move on to the next topic.'

questions.title: Aren't you overqualified for this position?
questions.answer: 64 Toughest Q8: an invitation to teach a new way of seeing it. You contribute right away, the company gets your training for free, you want the work, and you want a long-term commitment.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** The real worry is that you'll get bored and leave. Reassure them with genuine reasons you want *this* role, the benefits of your extra experience to them, and your commitment.

| Step | What to say |
| --- | --- |
| **Acknowledge** | Treat it as a fair question, not an accusation. |
| **Benefit to them** | Faster ramp-up, less training, mentoring others. |
| **Why you want it** | The work itself is what you want to do (e.g. hands-on verification rather than management). |
| **Commitment** | You're looking for a long-term fit and expect to grow here. |

### Sample answer
> I understand the concern. The way I see it, my background means I can contribute quickly with less ramp-up. For example, I've already built UVM environments and done formal CDC sign-off. What attracts me is the work itself, hands-on verification of complex IP, which is exactly what I want to be doing. I'm looking for a place to grow over the long term, and I'm confident that if I do this job well, more opportunities will follow here.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Flight risk.
- Whether you'll accept direction or the scope of the role.

### Pitfalls
- Getting defensive.
- Agreeing that you're overqualified.
- Bringing up salary.

### Follow-ups
- **Won't you be bored?** Every block has hard corner cases, and you'd go looking for them.
- **Would you accept the posted salary?** Say the fit and the learning matter most, then discuss later in the process.

questions.title: What are your career options right now? (Are you interviewing elsewhere?)
questions.answer: 64 Toughest Q12: position yourself as a desired commodity; mention you're exploring one or two other opportunities, with a light touch.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** They're asking how desperate you are. Present yourself as in demand without being coy: you're exploring a few serious options, and this one is your top choice for specific reasons.

| Step | What to say |
| --- | --- |
| **Honest but light** | "I'm in process with a couple of other semiconductor companies." |
| **Preference** | "This role is my first choice because [team / IP / methodology]." |
| **Timeline (if relevant)** | Mention deadlines politely if you have an offer with a deadline. |

### Sample answer
> I'm interviewing with a couple of other semiconductor companies for DV internships, but this role is my first choice because of [the interconnect verification work and the team's use of formal]. If I receive another offer with a deadline, I'll let you know so we can coordinate.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Your market value and how urgent your situation is.
- Your genuine interest in them.

### Pitfalls
- Lying about competing offers.
- Sounding desperate ('I have nothing else').
- Naming companies in a way that sounds like a threat.

### Follow-ups
- **Which companies?** Naming industries or types is usually enough; be honest if they press.
- **If you got both offers, which would you choose?** This one, and give your specific reasons.

questions.title: Why have you been out of work (or out of school/industry) so long? (Explain this gap.)
questions.answer: 64 Toughest Q13: emphasise factors that prolonged the search by your own choice (being selective, thinking through what you do best), plus industry conditions.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Say honestly what you did during the gap and frame it as deliberate: building skills, being selective about fit, or circumstances outside your control. Then pivot to your readiness.

| Step | What to say |
| --- | --- |
| **Fact** | State the gap and reason briefly (job search, study, military service, family, health). |
| **What you did** | Projects, courses, certifications. For DV: [personal UVM project, formal course]. |
| **Selective** | "I wanted the right role, not the first one." |
| **Readiness** | Now fully ready and up to date. |

### Sample answer
> After [finishing military service / my bachelor's], I took [several months] deliberately to strengthen my skills for verification. I built a UVM testbench for an AXI crossbar and learned formal CDC with JasperGold, because I wanted to apply to DV roles with real hands-on experience instead of just taking the first job that came along. That preparation is why I'm applying here now.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Whether there's a hidden problem.
- Whether your skills are current.

### Pitfalls
- Over-explaining or sounding defensive.
- Lying about dates.
- Personal details you don't need to share.

### Follow-ups
- **What did you learn in that time?** Point to concrete projects and skills.
- **Why didn't you accept earlier offers?** Fit and focus on DV, without bad-mouthing anyone.

questions.title: Tell me honestly about the strong and weak points of your boss (advisor, company, management team).
questions.answer: 64 Toughest Q14: never be negative; stress only the good points; the interviewer wants to see how loyal and positive you are.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** This is a loyalty test. Stress the positives sincerely. If pressed, describe a difference in style neutrally and what you learned, never criticism.

| Part | What to say |
| --- | --- |
| **Strengths** | "My advisor gives a lot of autonomy and very rigorous technical reviews." |
| **If pressed for a 'weakness'** | Frame as a style: "He's very busy, so I learned to make our meetings efficient with written agendas." |
| **Learning** | What you took from working with them. |

### Sample answer
> My advisor has been great for my growth. He gives me a lot of independence and his technical reviews are very rigorous, so my verification plans have become much better. He's also very busy with several projects, so I've learned to send a short written agenda before our meetings, which makes our time together really efficient. I'd call that a useful habit rather than a weakness.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Loyalty and discretion. Would you criticise them behind their back?
- Professional maturity.

### Pitfalls
- Airing dirty laundry, even when you're invited to.
- Obvious fake praise with no specifics.

### Follow-ups
- **What would you change about your lab?** A small, constructive improvement you could help with yourself.
- **What do you need from a manager?** Clear goals, regular feedback, and autonomy on how to do the work.

questions.title: What good books have you read lately?
questions.answer: 64 Toughest Q15: never fake familiarity; read a handful of recent, influential books in your profession and on management, plus a quality bestseller.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Never fake familiarity. Name one or two books you actually read that relate to your profession, plus optionally one quality general book, and say what you took from each.

| Choice | Example |
| --- | --- |
| **Professional** | e.g. *SystemVerilog for Verification* (Spear & Tumbush), *Formal Verification* (Seligman et al.), or *Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach*: only if you really read them. |
| **Takeaway** | One concrete idea you applied (e.g. using `bind` for assertions, coverage-driven methodology). |
| **Optional general** | A real non-fiction or fiction book; one line on why. |

### Sample answer
> Recently I've been reading [*Formal Verification: An Essential Toolkit for Modern VLSI Design*]. The chapter on [formal property verification for control logic] changed how I think about where to use formal versus simulation, and I tried it on my crossbar's arbiter. Outside work, I enjoyed [a real book you read], because [one sentence].

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Curiosity and continuous learning.
- Honesty: they may ask follow-up questions about the book.

### Pitfalls
- Naming a book you haven't read.
- Saying you don't read at all.
- Something controversial or shallow.

### Follow-ups
- **What did you disagree with in it?** Have one thoughtful point.
- **Any blogs, papers or podcasts?** Verification Academy, DVCon papers, specific tool docs.

questions.title: What are your outside interests?
questions.answer: 64 Toughest Q17: be well-rounded, not a drone, but don't suggest outside activities will interfere; gauge the culture; use it to counter stereotypes.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Show that you're well-rounded, with interests that suggest positive traits (discipline, teamwork, curiosity) and won't interfere with work. Be genuine.

| Element | Example |
| --- | --- |
| **Interest** | e.g. [running / badminton / hiking / music / open-source contributions]. |
| **Trait it shows** | Discipline, teamwork, curiosity, persistence. |
| **Keep it brief** | One or two items with one detail each. |

### Sample answer
> Outside of work I [play badminton with a club twice a week], which keeps me balanced and is a good team activity. I also like [tinkering with FPGA side projects / contributing to an open-source simulator], which is honestly an extension of what I enjoy at work, building things and seeing them run on real hardware.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Culture fit and balance.
- Whether outside commitments could compete with the job.

### Pitfalls
- Nothing ('I just study').
- Interests that sound like they'd take priority over work.
- Controversial topics.

### Follow-ups
- **How do you balance this with work?** Fixed time slots that don't conflict with deadlines.
- **What have you learned from [interest]?** Connect it to a work trait.

questions.title: I'm concerned you don't have as much experience as we'd like in [X]. (The "fatal flaw" question)
questions.answer: 64 Toughest Q18 (fatal flaw): be honest about the shortcoming, don't apologise, and show how it made you work harder. Q32 (light experience): agree it's important, show your strength may be greater than the resume suggests, and stress your unique combination of qualifications.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Agree that it matters, honestly admit the gap without apologising, show that your related strength is bigger than the resume suggests, and shift the focus to your overall combination of strengths.

| Step | Example |
| --- | --- |
| **1. Agree** | "Yes, [emulation / industry tape-out / UVM RAL] is important for this role." |
| **2. More than it looks** | Related experience: e.g. you used a register model concept in [project], or you built a regression flow at scale for the lab. |
| **3. Learning evidence** | You ramped on JasperGold in [X weeks]; give a concrete plan for the gap. |
| **4. Combination** | UVM + formal/CDC + design background together match their needs. |

### Sample answer
> You're right that [emulation] experience would be valuable here, and I haven't used an emulator directly. But some of the underlying skills carry over. I've built synthesizable-friendly testbench structures and a regression flow that our lab uses at scale. I also learn tools quickly: I went from zero to a clean JasperGold CDC sign-off in [X weeks]. Together with my UVM work on the AXI crossbar and my RTL background, I think I can contribute right away while I build up emulation experience.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- How you handle a weakness in your candidacy.
- Whether the gap is a real problem or can be learned.

### Pitfalls
- Getting defensive or apologising too much.
- Pretending you have experience you don't.
- Arguing that the requirement isn't important.

### Follow-ups
- **How would you ramp up?** Internal docs, a small starter task, and pairing with a senior.
- **Why didn't you get that experience before?** Explain your access in academia without making excuses.

questions.title: How do you feel about reporting to someone younger than you (or of a different gender, background, etc.)?
questions.answer: 64 Toughest Q19: avoid anything patronising; you admire companies that promote on merit; the person and the position both deserve respect.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Say sincerely that people should be respected for their competence. The person in the role earned it, and you'd be glad to work with and learn from them.

| Element | What to say |
| --- | --- |
| **Principle** | Merit-based environments are the best ones to work in. |
| **Respect** | Whoever holds the role earned it; both person and role deserve respect. |
| **Evidence** | You've worked well with [younger senior labmates / diverse teams]. |

### Sample answer
> It wouldn't make any difference to me. Whoever is in that role earned it, and I'd expect to learn from them. In my lab, some of the people I learned the most from were younger than me but had more verification experience, and I value working somewhere that promotes people based on what they can do.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Sincerity. Do you really mean it?
- Any hidden bias.

### Pitfalls
- Patronising lines ('some of my best friends are…').
- Over-elaborating, which can sound insincere.

### Follow-ups
- **Have you had a younger mentor?** Give a brief real example.
- **How do you handle disagreement with a manager?** Respectfully, with data, then commit.

questions.title: Can you tell us about confidential details of your current or previous employer (or lab)?
questions.answer: 64 Toughest Q20: never reveal anything truly confidential; explain diplomatically; some interviewers press only to test integrity, and only those who hold fast are hired.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Never reveal confidential information. Decline diplomatically, explain that you'd protect their information the same way, and describe your achievements in non-confidential terms.

| Step | What to say |
| --- | --- |
| **Decline politely** | "I want to be as open as I can, but that's under NDA / unpublished research." |
| **Principle** | You'd protect this company's information the same way. |
| **Offer what you can** | Talk about the methodology, the type of bug, and the outcome in general terms. |

### Sample answer
> I'd like to be as open as I can, but that design is [under an NDA with our industry partner / unpublished research], so I can't share specifics like the architecture or the bug details. What I can tell you is the methodology: I built a UVM environment with an ID-based scoreboard and used formal CDC checks, and it found [N] issues before freeze. I'd treat your company's information exactly the same way.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Integrity. Some interviewers press deliberately to test you (64 Toughest).
- Whether you can still describe your work usefully.

### Pitfalls
- Revealing anything under NDA, even if they keep pushing.
- Being so secretive you can't talk about your work at all.

### Follow-ups
- **Just roughly, what was the chip?** Stay general: 'a [type of] accelerator', only to the extent that's public.
- **Why should we trust you with our IP?** Because you just showed how you handle someone else's.

questions.title: Would you lie for the company?
questions.answer: 64 Toughest Q21: avoid choosing between two values; 'I would never do anything to hurt the company.' If pressed, always choose personal integrity.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Avoid a forced choice between loyalty and integrity with a positive statement. If pressed, always choose integrity.

| Part | What to say |
| --- | --- |
| **Positive statement** | "I would never do anything to hurt the company." |
| **If pressed** | "But I wouldn't lie. Long-term, honesty protects the company." |
| **DV angle** | e.g. you'd never mark a test as passing or waive a real bug to meet a schedule; you'd escalate the risk honestly. |

### Sample answer
> I'd never do anything to hurt the company, and I'd work hard to protect its interests. But I wouldn't lie, because in the long run that hurts the company more. In verification especially, my value is that people can trust my sign-off. If I ever reported coverage as closed or waived a real bug to hit a date, that trust would be gone. I'd raise the risk honestly and help find a real solution instead.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Integrity versus loyalty.
- Whether your judgement can be trusted.

### Pitfalls
- 'Yes, if needed.'
- Lecturing the interviewer.

### Follow-ups
- **What if your manager asked you to waive a failing test?** Ask why, document the risk, and escalate if it's a real bug.
- **Is it ever OK to waive a check?** Yes, with a documented, reviewed technical justification.

questions.title: Looking back, what would you do differently in your life or career? (If you could live your life over, what one thing would you change?)
questions.answer: 64 Toughest Q22: you're happy and fulfilled and wouldn't change a thing. Q39: generally happy with career progress; maybe would have moved toward a direction sooner if you'd known; take responsibility, no regrets. 1point3acres #7: name a turning point or missed opportunity (e.g. focusing on your career earlier) and show you're acting on it now.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Stay positive. You're generally happy with your path. If you name something, make it a minor missed opportunity you're already acting on, not a deep regret.

| Part | What to say |
| --- | --- |
| **Positive frame** | "I'm happy with my path; every step taught me something." |
| **One small change** | "I'd have started hands-on verification projects earlier in undergrad." |
| **Already acting** | Since then: AXI crossbar UVM TB, formal CDC, and seeking this internship. |

### Sample answer
> Overall I'm happy with my path. Each step taught me something useful. If I had to pick one thing, I'd have started hands-on verification work earlier. In undergrad I focused on coursework and only discovered how much I enjoy DV in my master's. I've been making up for it since, with the AXI crossbar UVM project and formal CDC work, and this internship is the next step.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Whether there are lingering regrets that affect your performance.
- Self-reflection and forward focus.

### Pitfalls
- Big personal regrets or disappointments.
- Anything implying you don't really want this career.
- Blaming others for how your path went.

### Follow-ups
- **Why didn't you start earlier?** You hadn't been exposed to DV yet. Keep it brief and positive.
- **How could you have improved your career progress?** Say the same thing: you're happy, and with hindsight you'd have started DV projects sooner.

questions.title: Could you have done better in your last job or project? Have you done your best work there?
questions.answer: 64 Toughest Q23: never be negative; 'with hindsight you can always find things, but nothing of major consequence'; if needed, cite external conditions. Q61: you always do your best, and your best is right now, like an athlete hitting their stride.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Say you always give your best and your best work is happening now, as your skills are compounding. If pressed for something you'd improve, name an external constraint or a small process lesson.

| Part | What to say |
| --- | --- |
| **Always best effort** | "I gave it my full effort, and I'm proud of the results." |
| **Hindsight lesson** | e.g. "With hindsight, I'd have written SVA protocol checkers earlier; I do now." |
| **Best is now** | Skills are compounding; your best work is ahead and you're hitting your stride. |

### Sample answer
> I gave that project my full effort and I'm proud of the result: [X%] coverage and [N] bugs found. With hindsight there's always something to improve. I'd have added protocol assertions on the interfaces from day one instead of halfway through, which I now do by default. But I'd say my best work is happening right now, because each project builds on the last.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Whether you hold back or have performance problems.
- Self-awareness without self-sabotage.

### Pitfalls
- Confessing major problems.
- Saying 'absolutely my best' (it sounds like you've peaked).
- Saying 'no' (it sounds like you didn't try).

### Follow-ups
- **What stopped you from doing better?** An external constraint, e.g. licence access or a spec change, and how you adapted.
- **What will your best work here look like?** e.g. owning a block from plan to sign-off.

questions.title: What makes you angry?
questions.answer: 64 Toughest Q25: suit the answer to your personality and the firm's style; even-tempered, communicate expectations, follow up; impatient only when there's no good reason for poor performance.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Come across as even-tempered but with standards. Frustration at things that hurt the team (dishonesty, unclear goals, avoidable rework), handled constructively.

| Part | What to say |
| --- | --- |
| **Temperament** | "I'm generally even-tempered." |
| **What frustrates you** | Avoidable problems: e.g. hiding a known bug, or not communicating a slip. |
| **How you respond** | Address it early and calmly with facts; focus on prevention. |

### Sample answer
> I'm generally pretty even-tempered. What frustrates me is avoidable problems, for example when someone knows about a bug or a schedule slip but doesn't say anything until it's too late. When that happens, I don't get angry at the person. I bring it up early and calmly, and suggest a process fix, like reporting status earlier or adding a regression check, so it doesn't happen again.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Emotional control.
- Your values, and whether you'd be difficult to work with.

### Pitfalls
- Coming across as a hothead.
- Saying 'nothing' (not credible, or it sounds like a pushover).
- Naming a trait that's common in the team or role.

### Follow-ups
- **When did you last get frustrated at work?** Give a short story with a calm resolution.
- **How do you calm down?** Step away briefly, then return to the facts.

questions.title: Is money important to you? (Why aren't you earning more at this stage of your career?)
questions.answer: 1point3acres #85/#86: salary commensurate with experience matters, but enjoying the work, fitting the culture and contributing matter more; not depending on money for happiness. 64 Toughest Q26: making money is important, but doing work you love at a company you respect matters even more.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Fair pay matters, but what you care about most is challenging work, learning, culture and contribution. Don't pretend money is irrelevant.

| Part | What to say |
| --- | --- |
| **Acknowledge** | "Fair compensation matters, it's part of the package." |
| **What matters more** | Interesting work, learning, team, impact. |
| **Tie to this role** | This role offers [X], which is why you applied. |

### Sample answer
> Fair compensation is important, and I'd expect it to reflect the market and my skills. But what drives my choices is the work itself. I want to be verifying complex designs, learning from strong engineers, and feeling that what I do actually matters. That's why I'm excited about this role, and I'm confident that if I do the work well, compensation will follow.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Motivation: money versus the work.
- Whether you'd leave for a small raise.

### Pitfalls
- 'Money doesn't matter to me at all' (not believable).
- Leading with money.
- Complaining about past pay.

### Follow-ups
- **What would make you happy compensation-wise?** Market-rate pay for the role; discuss specifics at the offer stage.
- **Job or salary, which is more important?** The job, as long as pay is fair.

questions.title: Who has inspired you in your life, and why?
questions.answer: 64 Toughest Q27: have a few heroes ready (a mental 'Board of Directors') and examples of how they inspired your achievements; highlight qualities valuable in the job.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Pick a real person whose qualities matter for this job (rigour, curiosity, mentoring) and give a specific example of how their influence shaped what you do.

| Element | Example |
| --- | --- |
| **Person** | e.g. [an advisor / a senior engineer / a professor / a well-known engineer]. |
| **Quality** | Rigour, patience in teaching, intellectual honesty. |
| **Concrete influence** | A habit you adopted from them (e.g. 'write the spec of your checker before coding'). |
| **Link to job** | Why that quality matters in DV. |

### Sample answer
> One person who inspired me is [my undergraduate digital-design professor]. He would never accept 'it works in simulation' as an answer. He always asked 'how do you know it's correct?' That question shaped how I work: I write down what my checker has to prove before I write the testbench, which is basically what a verification plan is. It's a big part of why I chose verification.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Your values and role models.
- Relevance to the job (64 Toughest: avoid irrelevant answers).

### Pitfalls
- Groping for a name, which suggests you've never been inspired.
- A long irrelevant story (e.g. a high-school coach) with no work link.

### Follow-ups
- **What did you learn from them that you still use?** Name the concrete habit.
- **Who do you look up to in the industry?** Have a real name with a real reason.

questions.title: Tell me about the most boring job (or task) you've ever had.
questions.answer: 64 Toughest Q29: you've never allowed yourself to be bored; there are challenges and problems in every job crying out for solutions.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Don't paint a memorable picture of boredom. Say you find a challenge in any task, and give an example of turning a dull task into something better, e.g. by automating it.

| Part | What to say |
| --- | --- |
| **Stance** | "I've rarely found a job boring; there's always a problem to solve." |
| **Example** | Repetitive task: manually checking regression logs. |
| **What you did** | Automated it: a Python log parser + summary report. |
| **Result** | Saved [X h/week]; became a lab tool. |

### Sample answer
> Honestly, I rarely find work boring, because there's usually a better way to do something if you look for it. For example, as a TA I had to check hundreds of students' simulation logs by hand. Instead of slogging through it, I wrote a Python script that parsed the logs and generated a summary, which cut the work from [several hours] to [minutes], and the next TA used it too.

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Your attitude toward routine work. DV has plenty of it, e.g. triaging regressions.
- Whether you'll stay engaged.

### Pitfalls
- Describing boredom vividly, so you become associated with it (64 Toughest).
- Complaining about a past employer.

### Follow-ups
- **How do you stay engaged in repetitive work?** Automate it, measure it, and look for patterns.
- **Do you enjoy regression triage?** Yes. It's pattern-finding, and automation makes it fast.

questions.title: Have you been absent from work (or school) more than a few days in any previous position?
questions.answer: 64 Toughest Q30: emphasise your excellent attendance record; if there was an issue, minimise it as an exceptional circumstance whose cause has been corrected.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** If not, emphasise your reliability and why showing up consistently matters. If yes, mention it briefly as an exceptional, resolved circumstance. Never lie.

| Case | What to say |
| --- | --- |
| **No issue** | "My attendance has always been solid; reliability matters to a team." |
| **If there was an issue** | "Other than [X weeks] in [year] for [resolved reason], I've had excellent attendance." |
| **Why it matters** | Teammates depend on you for drops, reviews, regressions. |

### Sample answer
> No. My attendance has always been consistent. In a project team, people depend on you for RTL drops, reviews and regression results, so being there and responsive matters a lot. [Alternative: Other than two weeks in [year] for a [medical matter that's fully resolved], my attendance has been excellent.]

### What the interviewer is assessing
- Reliability.
- Hidden attendance problems.

### Pitfalls
- Lying (it's easy to verify).
- Over-sharing medical or personal details.

### Follow-ups
- **Is the issue fully resolved?** Yes, and stop there.
- **How do you handle remote/hybrid reliability?** Clear status updates and fast response hours.
